content: Advancements in hepatitis B virus (HBV) detection technologies have created new opportunities to improve screening, referral, and treatment processes. This review aims to determine the most effective testing strategy for detecting hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) by evaluating diagnostic accuracy, cost, cost-effectiveness, and resource utilization. A comprehensive literature search was conducted using various databases and internet sources, focusing on HBV, screening, and testing strategies. Observational studies and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that provided original data from patient specimens were reviewed. The primary objective was to compare one-test strategies with two-test strategies for HBsAg detection. The search yielded 3,655 references from the literature and seven additional internet references. After screening titles and abstracts, seven articles were selected for potential data extraction. However, none of these articles met all inclusion criteria for final selection. As a result, no studies were identified that directly compared the diagnostic accuracy, cost, or cost-effectiveness of one-test versus two-test HBsAg testing strategies. The seven articles were further analyzed, with four providing national HBV testing algorithms (Australia, UK, US), one discussing testing strategies for specific populations, and two addressing the cost-effectiveness of certain testing strategies. Globally, an estimated 240 million individuals are chronically infected with HBV, with approximately 4 million acute infections occurring annually. HBV testing is essential for identifying infected individuals for treatment and care, referring uninfected individuals for vaccination, and mobilizing prevention and control efforts. Current guidelines focus on treatment eligibility, initiation of first-line therapies, switching treatments, and monitoring but lack specific recommendations on testing strategies, including which tests to use and how to implement them. This gap is particularly significant in lowand middle-income settings, where HBV testing guidelines are often limited or nonexistent. Chronic HBV infection is defined by the persistence of HBsAg for at least six months. The interpretation of HBV serologies is complex, with commonly used serological markers including HBsAg, total anti-HBc, and anti-HBs. The detection of HBsAg remains the most critical marker for diagnosing chronic HBV infection and determining the need for further assessment or treatment. Chronic HBV is confirmed by detecting HBsAg twice, six months apart. Following an initial positive HBsAg result, supplementary testing can facilitate entry into a care pathway. HBsAg detection methods include rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) and enzyme immunoassays (EIAs). Confirmation of a reactive HBsAg result typically involves either repeating the test with a different assay of similar sensitivity or performing a neutralization test using a specific anti-HBs-containing reagent. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends standardized testing strategies to maximize the accuracy of HBV and HCV testing while minimizing costs and increasing simplicity. This review addresses whether a single HBsAg assay provides sufficient specificity to proceed to supplementary testing or care or whether confirmatory testing with a different HBsAg assay (or neutralization) is required. This issue is particularly relevant in low-prevalence settings, where more than one assay may be necessary to confirm specificity. Two previous reviews on hepatitis testing focused on test performance but did not compare testing strategies. Testing strategies can involve a single HBsAg assay (e.g., RDT or EIA) or two-test strategies (e.g., a second RDT, EIA, or neutralization with EIA). The outcomes of interest include diagnostic accuracy, cost, cost-effectiveness, acceptability to healthcare workers and patients, and other outcomes such as missed cases of liver disease due to false negatives or unnecessary referrals and treatments due to false positives. The objectives of this review were to: 1. Identify quantitative evidence on the sensitivity and specificity of one-test versus two-test algorithms for HBsAg detection. 2. Evaluate the cost-effectiveness, acceptability, and other outcomes associated with these testing strategies. 3. Inform models to optimize HBV screening algorithms. The literature search was conducted by a medical librarian with expertise in systematic review searching. Databases searched included MEDLINE, EMBASE, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, Science Citation Index Expanded, SCOPUS, and others. The search was supplemented by internet searches for peer-reviewed articles, conference abstracts, and national guidance documents. The search was limited to English-language studies involving human subjects. The librarian search identified 3,655 references for PICO 3. After combining these with 3,060 references from a related search for PICO 4 (HCV), 2,388 references were excluded immediately. An additional 835 references were excluded for irrelevance, and 1,553 duplicates were removed, leaving 4,327 references for screening. Titles and abstracts were screened according to protocol inclusion and exclusion criteria. Ultimately, no reports met all eligibility criteria for data extraction to address the review question. Seven reports were assessed for eligibility, but none directly compared the cost or effectiveness of one-test versus two-test algorithms. Most of the literature focused on screening blood donations. The seven reports included: 1. A cost-effectiveness analysis of sequential HBeAg or HBV DNA testing in HBsAg-positive pregnant women. 2. Recommendations for HBV screening in high-risk populations by the US Preventive Services Task Force. 3. Development of recommendations for HBV screening by the US Preventive Services Task Force. 4. A cost-effectiveness analysis of HBV control strategies combining universal vaccination with immunoglobulin treatment. 5. UK standards for HBV diagnostic serology. 6. The Australian national HBV testing strategy. 7. An evaluation of HBsAg assay performance and testing algorithms using ELISA and other detection assays. None of the reports compared the cost or effectiveness of two different testing algorithms. Most studies focused on screening blood donations rather than broader testing strategies.
